section_summary: This section documents U.S. diplomatic, military-intelligence, and consular reporting on alleged Japanese surveying, mapping, fishing, intelligence, procurement, and propaganda activities in Mexico during 1932 and early 1933. Reports focus particularly on Sonora, Chihuahua, Baja California, and the Gulf of California, but repeatedly distinguish rumor and hearsay from verified evidence. A substantial portion concerns pro-Japanese, anti-American pamphlets and newspaper articles predicting a Japanese-American war and urging Mexico to side with Japan, along with investigations of Japanese fishermen and naval attaché Kohei Ochi.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for the Adjutant General: Japanese Activities in Mexico
subfiles.from: Alfred T. Smith, Colonel, General Staff, A.C. of S., G-2
subfiles.about: Directs follow-up investigation of reports that Japanese engineers were mapping strategic areas of Chihuahua near the United States border.
subfiles.summary: Memo recounts fourteen Japanese engineers west of Pearson, Chihuahua, relating it to Sonora and Pacheco activity; asks Eighth Corps Area to confirm and watch the border.

subfiles.title: Confidential Mail Instruction No. 540
subfiles.about: Notifies the ambassador of additional War Department communications concerning alleged Japanese activities in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Instruction No. 540: the War Department sent the military attaché a February 11 communication with a Fort Bliss report and a memorandum.

subfiles.title: Supplementary Confidential Mail Instruction No. 543
subfiles.about: Corrects the previous instruction concerning what the War Department sent to the embassy's military attaché.
subfiles.summary: Instruction No. 543 corrects that the February 11 communication was not sent; War forwarded a February 16 letter enclosing a February 2 Fort Bliss report.

subfiles.title: Confidential Mail Instruction No. 549
subfiles.about: Transmits Department of Justice material about alleged Japanese activities in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The instruction encloses a February 19 Department of Justice letter and a special agent's report. Page 75 is the associated file-number backer for record 894.20212/323.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division Distribution Sheet
subfiles.to: Internal military and State Department distribution
subfiles.about: Records internal routing of intelligence material to military branches and State Department divisions.
subfiles.summary: MID distribution sheet for the following intelligence report.

subfiles.title: Extract Copy of Report No. 3770: Japanese Activities in Mexico
subfiles.from: Robert E. Cummings, Acting Military Attaché
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese arrivals at Pacific ports and discusses a rejected Japanese colonization proposal.
subfiles.summary: Report No. 3770: Japanese groups landed at Guaymas with survey and photographic gear; 316 Japanese entered Pacific ports October 1931-January 1932; Solis says Mexican leaders opposed Japanese colonization.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 49 from Mexico City
subfiles.about: Seeks instructions concerning Robert Dunn's proposed trip to Sonora to observe Japanese engineering activity.
subfiles.summary: Clark says a naval reserve civilian, Dunn, will visit Sonora for Naval Intelligence; Mexican authorities might be irritated if they discover it, and he asks whether to notify them.

subfiles.title: Incident Involving Japanese Fishing Vessel Kamine and American Cannery Tender Vergana
subfiles.from: William A. Smale, American Consul, Ensenada
subfiles.about: Reports an American vessel's improper demand that a Japanese fishing vessel lower the Japanese flag and fly the American flag.
subfiles.summary: At sea the Vergana's mate, seeing San Diego on the Kamine's stern, ordered its Japanese master to fly the American flag; Smale avoided a publicized inquiry and suggested examining the vessels' home ports.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division Distribution Sheet
subfiles.to: Internal military and State Department distribution
subfiles.about: Provides an internal distribution list for intelligence correspondence.
subfiles.summary: MID distribution sheet for the following correspondence.

subfiles.title: Japanese Activities on the West Coast
subfiles.from: W. H. Simpson, Executive Officer, G-2
subfiles.to: Military Attaché, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Forwards intelligence excerpts and a translated anti-American article from El Noroeste.
subfiles.summary: MID letter sends excerpts of recent correspondence and a translated El Noroeste article described as Japanese propaganda; copies to State and Naval Intelligence.

subfiles.title: Excerpts from Recent Correspondence Received in Military Intelligence Division
subfiles.to: Secretary of War and Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2
subfiles.about: Compiles reports of purported Japanese military personnel, reconnaissance, migration, and fishing activity in Baja California, California, Sinaloa, and Sonora.
subfiles.summary: Sources allege fifteen Japanese army officers secretly mapped the coast from San Diego to Bahia Magdalena, well-to-do Japanese moved through San Diego and Ensenada, and Japanese apparently evacuated Sinaloa and Sonora.

subfiles.title: Letter Forwarding El Noroeste Article
subfiles.from: Gilbert Procter, Intelligence Officer, Camp Stephen D. Little
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Eighth Corps Area
subfiles.about: Forwards a translation of a vitriolic article about war between Japan and the United States.
subfiles.summary: Procter says Mexican newspapers ran several articles on a possible Japanese-American war; the February 2 El Noroeste article was the most vitriolic.

subfiles.title: War Between Japan and the United States Is Inevitable
subfiles.from: Attributed to Lt. Gen. Kiokatsu Satō
subfiles.about: Argues that conflict with the United States is inevitable and necessary for Japanese expansion and national survival.
subfiles.summary: Article: the US obstructs Japanese interests in Asia and humiliates immigrants; Japan's expansion is essential; diplomacy will fail and war is Japan's inevitable destiny.

subfiles.title: Confidential Mail Instruction No. 552
subfiles.about: Advises the ambassador that the War Department sent the military attaché correspondence and a translated newspaper article.
subfiles.summary: Instruction No. 552: a February 23 War Department letter transmits intelligence excerpts and a translation on Japan-US relations from Camp Stephen D. Little.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 51 from Mexico City
subfiles.about: Clarifies Robert Dunn's nonofficial status and authorizes him to travel as an ordinary tourist.
subfiles.summary: After consulting Herschel Johnson, Clark told Dunn that Captain Bagley regarded him as a tourist, not as an operative on a secret naval mission. Dunn said he would merely observe and listen. Clark therefore declined to notify Mexican officials and allowed him to proceed with a warning to be careful.

subfiles.title: Confidential Mail Instruction No. 577
subfiles.about: Transmits another Department of Justice special-agent report about alleged Japanese activities.
subfiles.summary: The instruction encloses a March 4 Justice Department letter and a February 25 special-agent report. Page 96 is the associated file-number backer for record 894.20212/329.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference to Despatch No. 1279
subfiles.about: Directs readers to another decimal-file location for a despatch concerning Japanese food purchases in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Clark's Despatch No. 1279: Japanese agents arrive seeking foodstuffs for the Japanese Army.

subfiles.title: Purchase of Foodstuffs by Japanese Agents in Mexico
subfiles.about: Forwards newspaper reports that Japanese commercial agents were buying Mexican food for the Japanese Army.
subfiles.summary: Clark encloses press items reporting Japanese agents at Mazatlán and Guadalajara or elsewhere in Jalisco. They were said to be purchasing large quantities of beans and other provisions for Japan's armed forces.

subfiles.title: They Propose to Procure Foodstuffs to Supply the Forces of Their Country
subfiles.about: Reports plans by Japanese commercial agents to purchase large quantities of Mexican food products for forces fighting in China.
subfiles.summary: The article claims that agents arrived at Mazatlán and other points in Sinaloa and Sonora to contract for shrimp, dried tomatoes, salt fish, chickpeas, and other provisions. It predicts economic benefits for Pacific-coast producers and says the merchandise would be shipped by a Japanese line serving American ports.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to the Attorney General
subfiles.from: James Grafton Rogers, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges a Justice Department neutrality report and notes that a redacted copy was sent to Mexico City.
subfiles.summary: Acknowledges the Attorney General's March 9 letter with Special Agent Bott's February 26 report, forwarded confidentially to the ambassador without Bott's name.

subfiles.title: Confidential Mail Instruction No. 579
subfiles.about: Transmits a Justice Department report that also mentions an alleged plot by Mexican generals.
subfiles.summary: The instruction encloses a March 9 Justice Department letter and a February 26 special-agent report on Japanese activities. It highlights allegations that Mexican generals, some reportedly in the United States, planned to overthrow Mexico's government. Page 104 is the associated file-number backer.

subfiles.title: File Backer 894.20212/332
subfiles.about: Marks the file position for record 894.20212/332.
subfiles.summary: The page contains only the decimal-file number. No substantive text survives in this section.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division Distribution Sheet
subfiles.to: Internal military and State Department distribution
subfiles.about: Lists offices to receive or review intelligence material.
subfiles.summary: MID distribution sheet preceding an April report on Japanese activity in Sonora.

subfiles.title: Japanese Activities on the West Coast of Mexico
subfiles.from: W. H. Wilson, Acting Executive Officer, G-2
subfiles.to: Military Attaché, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese naval captain's ceremonious visit to Mexican troops at Lomas and identifies him tentatively as Kohei Ochi.
subfiles.summary: Five Japanese led by a naval captain observed drills and filmed troops at Lomas, Sonora, honored by General Rico; Captain Kohei Ochi, bound to become naval attaché, was the likely visitor.

subfiles.title: File Backer 894.20212/334
subfiles.about: Marks the file position for record 894.20212/334.
subfiles.summary: The page contains only a decimal-file number and no substantive correspondence.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Summary of Despatch No. 1678
subfiles.about: Summarizes an embassy despatch on Japanese propaganda, Juan Mérigo, and arrested Japanese fishermen.
subfiles.summary: Memo on Despatch No. 1678: Merigo's pamphlet urges Mexico to fight the US, allegedly paid for by the Japanese minister; the arrest of five Japanese fishermen in Sonora connects to Gulf soundings reports.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1678: Japanese Propaganda and Activities in Mexico
subfiles.about: Forwards documents concerning pro-Japanese propaganda and the arrest of Japanese fishermen in Sonora.
subfiles.summary: Clark reports General Enriquez's plan to counter propaganda by the Japanese minister and Juan Merigo, whose pamphlet urges Mexico to join Japan against the US; encloses a monarchy defense and Ochi memorandum.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation with Simón Báez
subfiles.about: Records Simón Báez's request for embassy assistance in countering Japanese propaganda.
subfiles.summary: Baez says General Enriquez wants US material to rebut Japanese propaganda and that the Japanese minister paid Merigo $10,000 to print his pamphlet.

subfiles.title: Biographical Data of Ex-Brigadier General Juan Mérigo
subfiles.to: American Embassy and Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes Juan Mérigo's military career, political associations, and later business activities.
subfiles.summary: Biography of ex-General Juan Merigo: Madero and Carranza service, removal after opposing the Plan of Agua Prieta, failed Morocco attempt, chicle and banana interests, unproven Grey Automobile gang allegation.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for the Ambassador on Kohei Ochi and Hamaguchi
subfiles.from: Robert E. Cummings, Acting Military Attaché
subfiles.about: Reports conversations with Kohei Ochi about detained Japanese fishermen, alleged soundings, and Juan Mérigo's pamphlet.
subfiles.summary: Ochi questioned Cummings about Hamaguchi and four fishermen arrested in Sonora for soundings, repeating a claim an American agent paid for the arrests, which Cummings denied; Ochi admitted talking with Merigo but refused a publication loan.

subfiles.title: Report No. 4020 on La Guerra Yankee-Japonesa y la Actitud de México
subfiles.from: Robert E. Cummings, Acting Military Attaché
subfiles.about: Summarizes Juan Mérigo's pamphlet and assesses allegations that Japan funded its publication.
subfiles.summary: The report says Mérigo predicted an inevitable Japanese-American war and claimed that Mexico and numerous Latin American states would support Japan. It repeats Simón Báez's statement that the Japanese minister paid Mérigo $10,000, but Cummings doubts the allegation. He also observes that the pamphlet had little circulation in Mexico City.

subfiles.title: Biographical Data of Ex-Brigadier General Juan Mérigo
subfiles.about: Provides biographical information about pamphlet author Juan Mérigo.
subfiles.summary: Biography of Merigo: education, revolutionary service, army removal, Spain trip, Quintana Roo and Veracruz business ventures, unproven Grey Automobile allegation, uncertain livelihood in June 1932.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Note on Japanese Activities and the Kumano
subfiles.about: Summarizes intelligence reports and a Guaymas consular despatch about Japanese fishermen, mapping, and the seizure of the Kumano.
subfiles.summary: Note on Hamaguchi's arrest and the Kumano seizure: the Guaymas consul found no real evidence of Gulf charting; a Mexican general linked it to smuggling and said Mexico would side with the US.

subfiles.title: Report No. 4038: Japanese Activities in Mexico
subfiles.from: Robert E. Cummings, Acting Military Attaché
subfiles.about: Reports conversations with Kohei Ochi about Hamaguchi's arrest, Gulf soundings, and Juan Mérigo's propaganda.
subfiles.summary: Report No. 4038: Ochi says Hamaguchi and four fishermen were accused of soundings; Cummings denied US secret agents in Mexico and thinks Ochi knew more about Merigo than he admitted.

subfiles.title: Extracts on the Kumano Seizure and Japanese Dentist at Guadalupe y Calvo
subfiles.from: Commanding Officer, 25th Infantry, and First Cavalry Division
subfiles.about: Compiles reports on a seized Japanese fishing craft and a Japanese dentist allegedly mapping landing fields.
subfiles.summary: Extracts: Mexican soldiers seized the Kumano at Puerto Lobos without explanation; a Japanese dentist at Guadalupe y Calvo allegedly mapped landing fields and recruited laborers; second-hand.

subfiles.title: Japanese Activities in Mexico: Seizure of the Kumano
subfiles.from: L. B. Clapham, Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Eighth Corps Area
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department
subfiles.about: Forwards an Associated Press report that Mexican authorities seized the Japanese fishing vessel Kumano.
subfiles.summary: Clapham forwards a dispatch on Mexican authorities taking the Kumano to Guaymas without explanation, noting the vessel appeared in earlier reports.

subfiles.title: Alleged Activities of Japanese Craft
subfiles.from: A. F. Yepes, American Vice Consul, Guaymas
subfiles.about: Investigates rumors that the detained Kumano No. 5 and its Japanese crew were secretly charting the Gulf of California.
subfiles.summary: Yepes identifies five crewmen detained near the Colorado River and finds no support for naval charting rumors, since Gulf charts were commercially available; General Garay says they were investigated for smuggling and lacked fishing permits.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Note on San Luis Potosí Propaganda Incident
subfiles.about: Summarizes a consular despatch about pamphlet distribution at a Rotary Club dinner and a related newspaper article.
subfiles.summary: Note: a Japanese Rotarian distributed 'The Yankee-Japanese War and the Attitude of Mexico' at a club meeting, violating Rotary's ban on political activity; a newspaper interview predicted a Japanese-Soviet invasion.

subfiles.title: Anti-American Propaganda in San Luis Potosí Being Spread by Japanese Residents
subfiles.about: Reports Antonio Y. Kurachi's distribution of an anti-American pamphlet at a Rotary Club dinner.
subfiles.summary: Shaw says Kurachi distributed Merigo's pamphlet at an August 17 Rotary dinner; he objected, most members agreed it was improper, but it reached the press; he forwards an article predicting a Japanese-Soviet invasion.

subfiles.title: Remarks of Consul George P. Shaw at the Rotary Club Dinner
subfiles.about: Objects in Spanish to the use of the Rotary Club for distributing a pamphlet attacking the United States.
subfiles.summary: Shaw invokes Rotary's ban on political participation and asks the club to reprimand the member who distributed the pamphlet.

subfiles.title: Incident at the Rotary Supper of Last Night
subfiles.about: Reports the confrontation caused by Antonio Kurachi's distribution of Juan Mérigo's pamphlet.
subfiles.summary: Article: Kurachi distributed pro-Japanese, anti-American copies at the Hotel Progreso; Shaw objected and sought a formal clarification.

subfiles.title: Incidente en la Cena Rotaria de Anoche
subfiles.about: Spanish original of the report about the Rotary Club pamphlet incident.
subfiles.summary: Spanish article on Kurachi's pamphlet distribution and Shaw's protest, emphasizing respect for the US and Shaw.

subfiles.title: The Invasion of United States Territory by Oriental Forces Is Imminent
subfiles.about: Claims that Japan and Soviet Russia would soon unite to invade the United States.
subfiles.summary: Japanese army officer predicts Hoover's collapse and a joint Japanese-Soviet offensive, claiming veterans' treatment leaves the US weak.

subfiles.title: La Invasión de Territorio Norteamericano por Potencias Orientales es Inminente
subfiles.about: Spanish-language original of the article predicting a Japanese-Soviet invasion of the United States.
subfiles.summary: The clipping reproduces the claims translated on pages 144–145. It predicts resignations within the Hoover administration and portrays American labor and veterans as unwilling to support a coming war.

subfiles.title: Japanese Propaganda in the San Luis Potosí Consular District
subfiles.about: Reviews anonymous propaganda letters and a warning about an alleged Japanese military intelligence officer in San Luis Potosí.
subfiles.summary: Shaw reports a year of quiet Japanese propaganda, anonymous anti-American letters, and a January 30, 1933 letter alleging an attack on the Philippines between June and September; discusses Dickinson and Kurachi; continues beyond page 150.
